summary: Provides a scalable solution to the problem of distributing cryptographic keys to members of a multicast group. It is an experimental protocol.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 1949 describes how to securely give a secret group key to everyone in a multicast group without needing one central server to deliver it to each person individually. It does this by building on the Core Based Tree (CBT) multicast protocol.

questions: how to distribute keys for multicast
what is scalable multicast key distribution
how does cbt distribute multicast keys
what is a group key distribution centre
subtitle: Secure key distribution for multicast groups using CBT trees

tldr.problem: Multicast needs group keys distributed securely, but central key distribution doesn't scale for large, widely distributed groups.
tldr.mechanism: Using Core Based Tree (CBT) multicast, core routers authenticate joins and distribute keys as part of tree setup, delegating key distribution capability to routers along the path.
tldr.outcome: It provides a scalable, distributed approach to multicast key distribution. RFC 1949 is Experimental and CBT itself saw limited Internet-wide adoption.

facts.label: Key components
facts.value: Group session key, key-encrypting key (KEK), security parameters

facts.label: Trust model
facts.value: Routers on the tree are trusted (unless restricted to cores)

facts.label: IGMP requirement
facts.value: Requires modifications to IGMP v3 for secure join tokens

today: RFC 1949 is Experimental. CBT did not see widespread adoption in the Internet multicast landscape, where protocols like PIM became dominant. The distributed key management concepts it described influenced later work on multicast security.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
As multicast use grew (notably on the MBONE), there was a need for security services like integrity, authentication and confidentiality for multicast data. This requires securely distributing a group session key to all receivers.

The Core Based Tree (CBT) multicast protocol is well suited for this because it uses a hard-state shared tree per group with designated core routers. CBT makes security an integral part of the protocol, though its use is optional. CBT's key distribution mechanism does not require other multicast protocols to use CBT for data traffic.
sections.plainLanguage: To talk secretly in a big group, everyone needs the same secret key. CBT's tree structure naturally supports giving that key out safely as people join.

sections.title: The Multicast Key Distribution Problem
sections.content:
With a traditional Key Distribution Centre (KDC), the KDC generates the group key and must encrypt it separately for each receiver. For n receivers, this means n encryptions. For large, widely distributed groups, this doesn't scale well.

Even harder is per-sender authentication. To tell which sender sent a message, each sender needs a sender-specific key. Managing keys for every sender-receiver pair scales poorly.
sections.plainLanguage: If you have to wrap the same secret in a different envelope for every single person, it takes too long and uses too much effort for big groups.

sections.title: CBT Architecture and Security Advantages
sections.content:
CBT maintains hard state in routers, so each router knows its neighbours on the tree. Neighbours can be mutually authenticated during tree setup. The primary core router acts as the initial Group Key Distribution Centre (GKDC).

As routers join and are authenticated, key distribution capability can be delegated to them. This makes the scheme distributed rather than centralised. Because of hard state, routers don't need to repeatedly re-authenticate after inactivity unless there is a network failure.
sections.plainLanguage: In CBT, the main router can start off handing out keys. As more routers join the tree and prove who they are, they can help hand out keys too.

sections.title: Secure Tree Joining and Key Distribution
sections.content:
To join a secure group, a host sends an IGMP membership report with a digitally signed token. Its local designated router authenticates the token and forwards a signed CBT join request toward the primary core, carrying the host's token.

Each router along the path authenticates the request. At the primary core, both the router and originating host are checked against an access control list. If successful, the core creates a group access package containing the group session key, a key-encrypting key (KEK) for re-keying, and security parameters. The package is digitally signed and encrypted for the recipient.

The package travels back along the reverse path. Each intermediate router extracts its own encrypted key material and passes the host's encrypted key downstream. After receiving the acknowledgement, intermediate routers become GKDCs themselves.
sections.plainLanguage: When someone wants to join, routers along the path check their identity. The main router then sends back a locked box with the secret key. Each router keeps their own copy and passes the right box down to the next person.

sections.title: Sender-Specific Authentication
sections.content:
For existing group members who are senders, a sender can generate their own sender-specific key and security parameters, then multicast them to the group using the current group session key for encryption.

For non-member senders, the sender first negotiates security parameters directly with the primary core (using a protocol like Photuris or ISAKMP). The primary core then multicasts the new sender's session key and parameters to the group, encrypted with the group key. This allows receivers to authenticate messages from that specific sender.
sections.plainLanguage: If someone already in the group wants to prove their messages come from them, they can share a special key with everyone. If someone new wants to send, the main router can introduce them first.

sections.title: Status and Implementation
sections.content:
RFC 1949 is an Experimental protocol. A reference implementation of CBT with this security architecture existed at the time of writing. The proposal requires simple modifications to IGMP version 3 to support secure joins with digitally signed host tokens (described in Appendix B).

The model assumes routers on the delivery tree are trusted. For stricter security requirements, the RFC recommends that only core routers authenticate secure join requests, rather than all intermediate routers on the path.
sections.plainLanguage: This is an experimental idea. It works best if all the routers can be trusted. If not, you can restrict checks to just the main routers.
